lessons.lesson: The first live attempt remained gear-supported at about 773 rpm and 20 degrees collective. I also twice exceeded the 5 simulated-second command lease, then tried to use a stale observation and the action was rejected. Future decisions must renew controls early, use a slower explicit clock when reasoning is delayed, and cite a fresh observation. Collective demand and shaft speed alone do not guarantee takeoff.
basis: 20261031T060411-29e1d6 observations 69, 180, 329; decisions 1–3; rejected stale-observation feather request

lessons.lesson: On the proprietor-selected mission, low collective at about 1181 rpm unloaded the gear. At 20 degrees, an X-bank tendency appeared before full release. I reacted too late; the requested north/south correction was rejected as stale, and the craft rolled steeply and impacted. Recovery commands caused strong cross-axis rotation and tilt saturation. I must trim from measured response before leaving ground support, use body-frame rates after heading changes, and stop escalating commands when actuator feedback no longer follows targets. A clock-scale change also needs scheduler rebasing; 0.02x with a low-latency control transport is necessary for this pilot. This was a crash, not a completed A-to-B flight.
basis: observations 3174, 3203, 3261, 3288, 3308, 3333, 3358, 3414; actual decisions and rejected inputs

lessons.lesson: The lighter-airframe retry used smaller collective steps (12, 16, 18, 19.2, 20.3 degrees) and a north/south bias before loss of gear support. This produced a slow takeoff rather than the previous immediate roll crash, but does not isolate the effect of the lighter structure because my control behaviour also changed. I then over-corrected repeatedly: strong differential collective reversed roll rate rapidly, while observation-to-command delay and pitch lag made me release the correction too late. A 0.5-degree vector test produced unequal achieved nacelle angles and coupled body rates. I need to anticipate braking release from measured rate changes and account for actuator lag; merely reacting to bank angle is too late. The final approach contacted two feet while banked and sliding; the applied flare led to another airborne state. My last feather request was stale and rejected, and hosting shutdown ended the sortie. No stable landing or A-to-B success occurred.
basis: observations 660, 686, 702, 734, 751, 774, 791, 799, 811, 823, 846, 878, 902; 20 applied decisions; rejected feather; shutdown summary

lessons.lesson: With 10 kg initial fuel and the new bounded shaft regulator, the live test reached about 1181-1212 rpm under collective load, lifted free of all six feet at about 18 degrees mean collective, and stayed near A. My 1.5-degree north/south correction braked the negative X rate, but I still released too late: rate reversed and later reached plus 5.4 degrees per second. Reducing mean collective to 14.8 initiated descent; the delayed flare met the ground at about 1 m/s and contact induced a minus 15.35-degree-per-second X transient. This time I sent fresh feather/idle immediately after six-foot contact, and subsequent observations showed all six feet supported with near-zero GNSS velocity. I must release differential braking earlier from measured rate trend and begin descent flare sooner. A local contact-and-settle sequence is not completion of the proprietor's A-to-B mission, and these changes do not isolate fuel or governor effects from my changed inputs.
